assumptions: The compared velocities are signed on the same axis
Speeds sufficiently slow that elementary Galilean composition applies
The frame is suitably inertial for subsequent Newtonian force reasoning
conditions_and_limits: Relative velocities stated in different intermediate frames must be composed in order.
Do not add unsigned speeds automatically or infer meeting time without initial separation.
Individual displacement and path length need not be invariant under a moving frame; simultaneous separation and a meeting event are invariant under a common translation.
science_records.units_and_signs: Signed velocities in m/s, signed east positive.

science_records.claim: On a velocity-time graph, the signed area over a time interval is displacement, whereas total distance sums the magnitudes of segment contributions.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise v–t area and x–t slope
assumptions: The graphed quantities use a fixed coordinate system
Time interval is partitioned at genuine changes of velocity law
conditions_and_limits: Signed area is not automatically positive distance.
Vertical velocity jumps are idealizations; actual finite force implies finite-time change.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; signed area m; positive and negative velocities are directions.

science_records.claim: Each position formula applies only over the interval whose motion conditions define it.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise constant-velocity motion and interval-filtered intersections
assumptions: Correct start times and initial positions are known
Each interval's velocity law is valid only within declared bounds
conditions_and_limits: A solution outside its interval is inadmissible even if the algebra is correct.
After a stop, reversal or delayed departure, use a new position expression with continuity at the boundary.
science_records.units_and_signs: Global clock t in s; positions m; each segment retains signed velocity m/s.

science_records.claim: Over a time interval, average speed is total path length divided by duration; average signed velocity is net displacement divided by duration.
science_records.law_or_model: averages from path length and signed position
assumptions: One global start and end time
Correct distinction between path length and signed position
conditions_and_limits: Replacing displacement with path length in average velocity is invalid.
An object may have zero average velocity while having nonzero average speed.
science_records.units_and_signs: Speed ≥0, velocity has sign, both measured in m/s; length in metres and duration in seconds.

science_records.claim: For motion split into constant-velocity intervals, total distance is the sum of |v_i| Δt_i and net displacement is the sum of v_i Δt_i.
assumptions: Each stage's signed velocity and interval duration are defined
Each interval is counted once and no time gap is overlooked
conditions_and_limits: The magnitude of net displacement never exceeds total distance.
A reversal makes the algebraic displacement sum differ from summed distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; sums produce metres.

science_records.claim: For a straight-line segment on an x–t graph, signed slope Δx/Δt equals the constant velocity in that interval.
science_records.law_or_model: position-time slope and inverse graphical reconstruction
assumptions: Position and time axes have known scale and units
Motion is piecewise constant velocity for straight graph segments
conditions_and_limits: A horizontal x–t segment means rest in that frame, not zero position.
Graph height on x–t is position, whereas graph height on v–t is velocity.
science_records.units_and_signs: Position in m; time s; slope m/s.

science_records.claim: For a fixed straight axis, a uniformly spaced reading r maps to physical position x=b+kr, with nonzero signed scale k. Changing origin or direction changes coordinates, not physical separation.
assumptions: Straight stationary reference axis; uniform scale; both markers refer to the same physical points.
conditions_and_limits: Two distinct calibrated markers determine b and k only under the uniform-scale assumption.
A moving origin requires a time-dependent transformation; nonuniform scales require more information.
science_records.units_and_signs: x in m, r in scale divisions, k in m/division; sign of k gives axis orientation.

science_records.claim: Total path length D is at least |x_f−x_i|; in a straight monotone interval D=|Δx|. For a piecewise monotone route D is the sum of the absolute changes between all actual turns.
science_records.law_or_model: One-dimensional path-length ledger and endpoint lower bound
assumptions: Positions use one fixed metre axis; all stated turning points are included for an exact ledger.
conditions_and_limits: Finite position samples alone generally give only a lower bound.
An exact upper bound cannot be inferred without additional restrictions on unobserved motion.
science_records.units_and_signs: Positions and signed displacement in m; path length D≥0 in m.

science_records.claim: Average acceleration is Δv/Δt; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of v–t. In one dimension, nonzero v and a of the same sign increase speed, opposite signs decrease speed.
assumptions: Fixed one-dimensional axis; elapsed time positive; instantaneous sign criterion applies where velocity is nonzero.
conditions_and_limits: An interval average does not imply constant acceleration.
At a reversal v passes through zero; direction of acceleration is not itself direction of motion.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; acceleration m/s²; east-positive unless declared.

science_records.claim: For constant signed acceleration on an interval, v=u+at, Δx=ut+½at²=½(u+v)t, and v²=u²+2aΔx.
assumptions: Constant acceleration on the stated interval; one fixed coordinate axis; t is elapsed time since interval start.
conditions_and_limits: v² relation loses sign information; recover sign from time/domain.
Displacement is not distance when velocity reverses.
Variable acceleration needs a different model or piecewise intervals.
science_records.units_and_signs: u,v m/s; a m/s²; t s; Δx m.

science_records.claim: For uniform circular motion at radius r and period T, speed is 2πr/T; velocity is tangent and changes direction. Displacement is the endpoint vector, not arc length.
science_records.law_or_model: Uniform circular motion, arc length and vector displacement
assumptions: Fixed circle radius, fixed centre and constant speed; motion in a plane; defined orientation.
conditions_and_limits: Whole-revolution displacement is zero but speed is not.
Average velocity is the vector displacement divided by elapsed time; not the average of speed magnitudes.
Quantitative centripetal acceleration/force is an extension; no force law is needed here.
A uniform circular motion velocity vector changes direction; the instantaneous acceleration is inward even though the speed is constant.
science_records.units_and_signs: r in m, T in s; speed m/s; x and y east/north in m.

science_records.claim: Rotated orthonormal axes change components but not magnitude or physical separation; a range constraint may admit two reflected orientations.
science_records.law_or_model: Common-plane Cartesian vectors and triangle geometry
assumptions: Fixed common origin or explicitly translated origins; perpendicular axes; common length units.
conditions_and_limits: Independent signed coordinate or orientation evidence can resolve reflection ambiguity.
Two endpoint ranges p and q admit separation d only if |p−q|≤d≤p+q.
science_records.units_and_signs: m and degrees relative to named axis; east and north positive.

science_records.claim: External gears have equal tooth passage rates and opposite senses. A coaxial spool has the wheel frequency and winds or unwinds 2πr per turn.
assumptions: Fixed tooth counts, external meshing, no slip, constant spool radius, taut inextensible string.
conditions_and_limits: Each mesh reverses rotation sense; winding orientation fixes string-motion sign.
Force/energy calculations are separate topic work.
science_records.units_and_signs: rev/s, radius m, velocity m/s; clockwise sign and winding orientation declared.

core1a.phenomenon: Two surveyors mark the same corridor from opposite ends; their labels differ but the physical location of each marker does not.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A coordinate is a label for position relative to a chosen origin and direction. To compare readings from different rulers, first identify shared physical markers. A uniform ruler has a constant signed scale: subtract two paired readings to cancel the offset and determine the scale. One anchor then determines the offset. This explains why a shift of origin does not change displacement and why reversing an axis reverses its signed component. The physical separation remains the absolute difference in calibrated metre coordinates. Calibration is a model: two marks alone do not establish that every intermediate mark on a damaged ruler is equally spaced. A third independent check can invalidate the assumption. This is distinct from measuring the length of the travelled path. A rotated frame can be reconstructed with two distance equations. For endpoints on two circles, subtract equations to find the common x-coordinate, then keep both signs of y. A separate bearing or signed coordinate can remove the reflection ambiguity. Example: ranges 5 from origin and √10 from (3,0) give x=4, y=±3. Both satisfy the ranges; only a northing observation chooses y=+3. Apply a stated rate after normalizing units. Map v_i and v_f with signs; convert km/h by 5/18, m/min by 1/60, ms by 1/1000, and minutes by 60. Subtract velocities only in the same unit. Example: −36 km/h to +180 m/min in 4000 ms becomes −10 to +3 m/s in 4 s, so a_avg=+13/4 m/s². Multiply by 4 s to recover +13 m/s. This rate does not prove acceleration was constant.

core1a.phenomenon: A delivery robot visits recorded checkpoints, but its tracker may miss a detour between them.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A signed position change is determined by the initial and final points alone. Distance depends on the route: every piece of actual motion contributes a nonnegative length. Break a straight route at each real reversal, not just at each convenient recording time. Adding signed changes cancels intermediate positions, whereas adding their magnitudes preserves travel. The triangle inequality establishes the endpoint lower bound. If the logger records only some checkpoints, the sum of successive absolute changes is itself a lower bound; an unobserved turn can add distance without changing any sampled position. If motion is monotone between checkpoints, the bound is attained. This distinction matters when interpreting logs, inferring unknown turning positions, or testing claims about an incomplete journey. For perpendicular legs a,b, distance=a+b, displacement magnitude=√(a²+b²). If first direction is (c,s), a left turn gives (−s,c), so endpoint is (ac−bs,as+bc). Example: 3 m then 4 m gives length 7 and displacement magnitude 5; reversing the lengths can give the same endpoint with a different orientation. Solve both orders before using an independent turn observation. In one dimension, define P and N as positive and negative path magnitudes. Then D−|Δ|=2 min(P,N). This is an algebraic warrant valid for every finite log; equality holds iff one directional total vanishes. It permits rests and variable speed. Example: east 5 m in 1 s and east 2 m in 4 s has D=|Δ|=7 but different speeds. In a plane the triangle inequality is the warrant; equal sign of one component alone is insufficient.

core1a.phenomenon: A commuter can end near the starting point after a long journey: the speedometer and displacement tell different stories.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A description of motion begins with position, not the answer to a numerical formula. Mark the commuter's origin and east-positive coordinate. Each trip leg changes the position by a signed amount, but each contributes a positive path length. Average speed is the accumulated path length divided by elapsed time; average velocity is the single net position change divided by the same time. The two averages can differ even for a perfectly continuous trip, and average velocity becomes zero on a round trip. Reversing the coordinate direction reverses the velocity component without changing any physical speed. Build both numerical sums from the travel log before deciding which one the experiment measures. A graph of position versus time makes the change in direction visible, while a ledger of distances preserves how far the person actually travelled. When distance D and displacement Δ are measured for east and west legs, E=(D+Δ)/2 and W=(D−Δ)/2. Convert km/h by 5/18, m/min by 1/60, then time=leg length/speed. Example D=100 m, Δ=60 m, speeds 4 and 2 m/s: E=80, W=20, moving time=20+10=30 s. If elapsed=50 s, rest=20 s; a recorded 15 s rest is inconsistent. For two intervals, A=(s1t1+s2t2)/(t1+t2). Subtracting the unweighted mean gives (s1−s2)(t1−t2)/(2(t1+t2)). This establishes equality iff speeds or durations agree. Equal distances do not imply equal times. Example: 12 m at 2 m/s then 12 m at 6 m/s takes 6+2=8 s, giving 3 m/s, not 4. Including an additional rest changes the elapsed denominator. For equal out-and-return distances d at constant water-relative speed v and current c, the ground speeds are v+c and v−c. A return requires 0≤c<v. Moving time is d/(v+c)+d/(v−c)=2dv/(v²−c²); elapsed time includes any dwell. Worked anchor: d=120 m, v=4 m/s, c=2 m/s gives moving times 20 s and 60 s, total 80 s. A 10 s wait makes 90 s elapsed; average speed is 240/90, not (6+2)/2. To infer c from a clock, subtract dwell first and reject nonreal or domain-invalid results. This is a current/relative-velocity model, not a general law of wind-driven boats.

core1a.phenomenon: A trolley rolling west slows, stops and rolls east when a steady eastward acceleration acts.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Velocity specifies speed and direction; acceleration measures how velocity changes, not merely whether speed increases. On a fixed east-positive axis, an object with negative velocity can have positive acceleration: initially it slows, then it may reverse. Divide the signed change in velocity by elapsed time to obtain average acceleration. Only with a constant-acceleration model is this also the value throughout the interval. To determine speed change, compare the signs of instantaneous velocity and acceleration. If both have the same sign, the magnitude of velocity grows; if they have opposite signs, it shrinks. At zero velocity the sign rule needs care: the next interval determines the direction of motion. A velocity-time graph separates velocity sign (height), acceleration sign (slope) and a reversal (crossing zero). Acceleration–time signed area equals velocity change. Carry each boundary velocity into the next stage; integrate signed velocity to obtain displacement. Inverse readings constrain the switch time and acceleration together, with direction and feasibility checks. Under uniform acceleration a=(v_f−v_i)/Δt and v=v_i+a t_local. A reversal does not change the sign of a unless the acceleration changes. Speed decreases while velocity and acceleration have opposite signs. Example: v_i=−8, v_f=+4 in 6 s gives a=+2, zero after 4 s; speed decreases for 4 s, then increases. Check a×6=12. For several stages, the total average is net Δv divided by total elapsed time. Zero acceleration at every instant implies constant velocity over a connected interval. Zero average acceleration only fixes equal endpoint velocities. For example, v rises linearly from 1 to 4 m/s in 2 s and returns to 1 in 2 s: average acceleration zero, velocity variable. Negative acceleration decreases speed only while velocity is positive; with negative velocity it increases speed. If acceleration is continuous and nonnegative, zero accumulated change forces zero acceleration throughout. EXPLAIN is a causal chain, not merely a verdict. For one-dimensional motion with a>0, signed velocity increases. If v starts negative, its magnitude decreases until v=0; after v becomes positive its magnitude increases. The speed minimum follows from the sign change, not a reversal of acceleration. At v=0 the acceleration may remain nonzero. If acceleration is switched to zero at the zero-velocity event, the body remains at rest under that new condition. State each link and its warrant: acceleration controls signed velocity change; speed is magnitude; zero crossing changes which sign branch defines the magnitude. For two projectiles launched from one height with the same constant g, choose one downward-positive axis and use H=u_i t_i+gt_i²/2 for each. Equal depth is an equation, not permission to equate launch speeds. Worked anchor: one starts at rest, reaches a lower sensor at 3 s with g=8 m/s², so H=36 m. Another launched upward at 5 m/s reaches that depth when −5t+4t²=36; retain the positive root and check it follows the turn. The shortcut u=g(t₂−t₁)/2 holds only for equal opposite magnitudes.

core1a.phenomenon: A vehicle's recorded position can pause, rise or fall while time keeps increasing; the slopes tell its signed motion.
core1a.scientific_narrative: To read a motion graph, first name both axes. The height of an x–t graph is position, not speed. A horizontal x–t segment means that position is temporarily unchanged, whereas an upward slope means positive signed velocity and a downward slope means negative signed velocity. To obtain a velocity–time graph from a piecewise linear position record, compute the slope for every valid interval and place that signed velocity on the corresponding time segment. Conversely, the signed area under a velocity–time curve reconstructs each position increment, so the endpoint is independently checkable. For distance, however, the magnitudes of areas are added. Crossing the horizontal position axis does not necessarily mean the vehicle has stopped; the slope at that crossing decides velocity. Changing the coordinate origin shifts the whole x–t graph vertically without changing any velocity–time segment. This is a core representation-invariance check. A finite position table alone does not determine instantaneous slopes or hidden reversals: explicitly state linear interpolation or another valid motion model. On a straight velocity–time segment, find area using a rectangle, triangle or trapezoid; if the segment crosses zero, split at that instant for the distance ledger. For a position sketch, velocity at each instant supplies its tangent slope. This area-based construction prepares the constant-acceleration equations taught in M06. Distance and signed displacement determine opposite-sign areas P=(D+Δx)/2 and N=(D−Δx)/2. Similar triangles connect the unknown duration and final velocity to the zero crossing; validate the reconstructed graph against both observations. For any integrable velocity history, signed area is displacement and absolute area is distance. If v≥0 everywhere, both coincide. Equal area does not constrain slope: constant 2 m/s over 4 s and a line from 0 to 4 m/s over 4 s both have area 8 m, but accelerations differ. A line from −2 to +6 over 4 s has the same signed area, yet a negative triangle of 1 m makes distance 10 m. State the condition whenever turning equal signed areas into equal distances. A velocity change acquired early affects more of the subsequent position history than the same change acquired late. For example, two carts start at 2 m/s; one increases speed by 3 m/s early, then coasts, while the other acquires the same increase later. Their final speeds agree because their signed acceleration areas agree. The early cart carries its extra velocity for longer; its v–t area is larger, hence it has larger displacement. If the same change is a reduction, the ordering reverses. This is the missing causal bridge between a–t and x–t. Swapping two acceleration stages changes when velocity is acquired. For durations p,q and rates a,b, the endpoint velocity u+ap+bq is invariant. For the first ordering, x_X=up+ap²/2+(u+ap)q+bq²/2; reverse ordering yields x_Y=uq+bq²/2+(u+bq)p+ap²/2. Thus x_X−x_Y=(a−b)pq. This exact warrant says nothing by itself about total distance: |v| must be integrated separately when signs differ. A reversal-free nonnegative condition licenses distance=displacement; without it, construct opposite-direction equal-path examples.

core1a.phenomenon: A ball rolls up a ramp, momentarily stops, and rolls back; the same position may be visited at two distinct times.
core1a.scientific_narrative: For a constant signed acceleration, the velocity graph is a straight line. Its slope gives v=u+at. The signed area of the rectangle of height u and triangle of height at gives Δx=ut+½at², even when part of the graph lies below the axis. The trapezoid expression uses the arithmetic mean of endpoint velocities only because the graph is linear. Multiplying v−u=at by v+u and substituting the area gives v²−u²=2aΔx, without dividing by a. Squaring loses velocity sign, and a position equation can yield two legitimate times when a cart passes a point on either side of a reversal. Treat roots as candidate times until the stage domain, direction and endpoint are checked. Find total distance by splitting at any zero of velocity, not by taking the absolute value of total displacement. Use a separate signed motion law in each region; carry position and velocity through a boundary unless an impact is specified. If entering with speed u>0 and acceleration −k, the same boundary is revisited after 2u/k, with velocity −u. Penetration is u²/(2k). For u=6 and k=2, turn after 3 s at depth 9 m, return after 6 s; the two traversals contribute 18 m path but zero displacement. For constant acceleration, v²=u²+2aΔx determines speed squared, not automatically the signed velocity. If u=+8 m/s, a=−2 m/s² and Δx=12 m, v²=16 so v=±4. The relation v=u+at gives times 2 and 6 s; both describe the same position if the model lasts that long. At Δx=16 the roots merge at the turn. Negative v² means the position is inaccessible, not an imaginary physical speed. The half-distance comparison needs shared elapsed time, shared initial speed and uniform braking to zero. Under these hypotheses the braking velocity graph is a triangle of area uT/2; the constant-speed graph is a rectangle uT. A coast fraction q followed by braking gives ratio (1+q)/2. Equal area alone cannot prove constant acceleration: any nonnegative graph satisfying v(t)+v(T−t)=u has half-area, including nonuniform symmetric piecewise-linear histories. In the two-stage braking model with shared initial u and total T, switch time τ and switch speed w, distance=(uτ+wT)/2. Half reference distance is equivalent to w=u(1−τ/T); both segment slopes then equal −u/T. This is a valid converse only with exactly two linear segments and nonnegative velocity. With three intervals the same total area can be achieved by unequal slopes: complementary speeds v(t)+v(T−t)=u guarantee half-area. An explicit counterexample tests why the model restriction is necessary. For delayed interception, reset elapsed time at the pursuer's start. If target position relative to the start is D+Vs+As²/2, constant pursuer speed required for contact is D/s+V+As/2 for s>0. An unrestricted minimum for D,A>0 occurs at s=√(2D/A), but a finite time window may exclude it. Compare required speeds over the actual domain; endpoint contact can be optimal. Worked anchor: D=9 m, V=1 m/s, A=2 m/s² gives required speed 1+s+9/s, minimum 7 m/s at s=3 s when allowed; with a 2 s window the smallest speed is 7.5 m/s at closure. Check the interval before interpreting a double root.

core1a.scientific_narrative: The ground and a uniformly moving observer can assign different positions and velocities to the same object. In a common one-dimensional axis, x_rel=x_object−x_observer and v_rel=v_object−v_observer. These differences follow by subtracting the observer position at the same time; a constant observer velocity shifts every v–t segment by the same amount. A simultaneous separation between two objects and their meeting event are invariant under this shared translation, but an individual object's displacement and path distance need not be. For piecewise motion, build each position law from its actual boundary position and use one global clock. Solve for equality only on the interval where both laws apply. Match it to the receiver position in each stage. Example L=50 m, c=20 m/s; receiver travels east 4 m/s for 2 s then rests at x=8. Constant-speed root 100/24 is after 2 s, invalid; stationary return t=(100−8)/20=4.6 s, after reflection at 2.5 s.

core1a.phenomenon: A rider on a merry-go-round has a constant speedometer reading but changes direction continuously.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A circular path differs from a straight line because direction changes even when the speed is fixed. Take a circle with radius r, centre at the origin and east/north axes. A full revolution covers circumference 2πr; dividing by the period T gives constant speed. For a fraction f of a revolution, arc length is f(2πr), but displacement is the straight vector from initial to final point. Velocity at every point is tangent, perpendicular to the radius; for counterclockwise travel the tangent turns counterclockwise as the radius does. After one complete revolution the vector displacement and average velocity are zero, though the distance and speed remain positive. The changing velocity direction means acceleration exists. To see the direction of acceleration, draw two equal-length tangent velocity arrows at neighbouring points, with their tails together. Their vector difference points approximately toward the centre at the midpoint of the short arc. As the time interval shrinks, this direction approaches the inward radius at the current point; quantitative centripetal acceleration and forces are enrichment or PH02 material, not required to solve these tasks. No slip means N_A f_A+N_B f_B=0 using signed clockwise frequencies. Every external mesh reverses direction. A coaxial spool shares its gear's frequency, not the gear rim's linear speed. Example: 12 teeth driving 24 at 4 rev/s produces −2 rev/s at driven wheel. A 0.05 m spool moves string at 2π(.05)×2=.2π m/s; sign depends on winding. Opposite rotation stages can cancel height change but add to path. For uniform rotation, f=n/Δt, T=1/f, v=2πrf and arc=2πrn. Convert angular degrees to turns by dividing by 360. For radius 0.12 m and 270° in 0.5 s, n=.75, f=1.5 Hz, T=2/3 s, v=.36π m/s and arc=.18π m; the remaining three-quarter turn gives endpoint chord .12√2 m, not the arc. At constant nonzero circular speed, a rim marker's tangent rotates. Equal magnitudes do not make successive vectors equal: subtract nearby tangents to obtain a small inward-directed change (toward the midpoint radius, then toward the instantaneous centre in the small-time limit). Since acceleration is the rate of vector change, it is nonzero despite constant speed. After a complete revolution the velocity vector returns to its initial value, so its full-lap average acceleration is zero. A straight constant-velocity comparison isolates direction change as the reason. On a closed track of circumference L, two signed unwrapped arc coordinates sA,sB denote the same point exactly when sA−sB=kL for integer k. Keep each velocity regime and its time domain. Worked anchor: L=40 m, A starts at 0 with +3 m/s, B at 10 with −1 m/s. Relative coordinate −10+4t reaches 0 at 2.5 s and 40 at 12.5 s. If a direction switch occurs, carry the relative coordinate continuously to the switch and search multiples separately. A first positive contact may occur at k≠0.

stages.diagnose: Identify the earliest divergent model: circle phase or tangent, calibration, path versus displacement, time origin, acceleration validity, graph translation or relative separation.

stages.boundary_test: If O stays stationary at x=−2 m from t=6 onward instead, reconstruct the relative position and velocity tables and their displacement.

core1b.fresh_task: A cart completes one uniform lap of a radius-3 m circle in 6 s, entering an east-positive straight rail tangentially at the start point. The rail marker scale reads r=5 at x=0 and r=1 at x=8 m. Rail elapsed time s begins at zero when A enters. It accelerates uniformly for 4 s, then an odometer reports that its total circle-plus-rail travel is 6π+4π+8 m; the rail motion was eastward throughout. Determine A's rail acceleration, final velocity, position and marker reading. Cart B starts at rail x=4π+12 m and moves west at 1 m/s from s=0. Determine the first meeting during 0≤s≤4, checking the domain, and find whole-trip average speed and east-average velocity. Assume point carts do not interact.
core1b.protected_work: Combine circular speed and distance, calibrated coordinates, odometer path constraint, constant acceleration and relative position equations, then verify graph area and meeting domain.

stages.predict: Predict whether the odometer can isolate the straight-stage displacement if that stage never reverses.
stages.attempt: A cart completes one uniform lap of a radius-3 m circle in 6 s, entering an east-positive straight rail tangentially at the start point. The rail marker scale reads r=5 at x=0 and r=1 at x=8 m. Rail elapsed time s begins at zero when A enters. It accelerates uniformly for 4 s, then an odometer reports that its total circle-plus-rail travel is 6π+4π+8 m; the rail motion was eastward throughout. Determine A's rail acceleration, final velocity, position and marker reading. Cart B starts at rail x=4π+12 m and moves west at 1 m/s from s=0. Determine the first meeting during 0≤s≤4, checking the domain, and find whole-trip average speed and east-average velocity. Assume point carts do not interact.
stages.reconstruct: Loop path 6π, speed π m/s; rail path=4π+8, equal to signed Δx because rail motion eastward. Δx=4π+8=4π+½a·16, so a=1 m/s²; v(4)=π+4. x(4)=4π+8; scale x=10−2r, so r=1−2π. B(s)=4π+12−s; at s=4 B=4π+8=A(4). Closing speed π+s+1>0 throughout, so first meeting is exactly s=4. Rail v–t trapezoid area (π+(π+4))4/2=4π+8. Whole-trip path 10π+8, elapsed 10 s, average speed π+0.8 m/s; loop displacement zero, east average velocity (4π+8)/10 m/s.
stages.diagnose: Identify the earliest divergent model: circle phase or tangent, calibration, path versus displacement, time origin, acceleration validity, graph translation or relative separation.
stages.repair: Reconstruct the circle and straight-stage ledgers separately, then join them using the shared tangent speed, correct time origin, signed position and a valid meeting model.
stages.boundary_test: If B starts 2 m farther east with all other conditions unchanged, is there a meeting within the rail stage?

core1b.fresh_task: A rail survey logger uses a uniform scale r. Its marks r=2 and r=8 correspond to ground positions x=18 m and x=6 m (east positive). A third mark r=10 is reported at x=1 m. Decide whether all three reports can use one uniform calibration, and locate r=5 under the two-anchor model.
core1b.protected_work: Select and test a uniform signed coordinate model rather than treating instrument readings as metre positions.

stages.predict: Predict whether larger logger readings mean eastward or westward motion.
stages.attempt: A rail survey logger uses a uniform scale r. Its marks r=2 and r=8 correspond to ground positions x=18 m and x=6 m (east positive). A third mark r=10 is reported at x=1 m. Decide whether all three reports can use one uniform calibration, and locate r=5 under the two-anchor model.
stages.reconstruct: k=(6−18)/(8−2)=−2 m/division; b=18−(−2)(2)=22 m. Thus x=22−2r; r=5 gives 12 m, while r=10 predicts 2 m, not 1 m. Exact observations cannot all fit a single uniform calibration; this does not identify which observation failed.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the zero, signed scale, coordinate conversion or consistency check.
stages.repair: Use two common anchors to infer signed scale and offset, then test the extra independent observation.
stages.boundary_test: If the third mark instead gives x=2 m, what can and cannot be concluded about the model?

core1b.fresh_task: A robot visits markers at times 0, 2, 5 and 7 s. Scale A has its zero at ground x=4 m, increases east and uses 2 m per division. Its readings are −1, 3, 3, 0. Scale B has zero at ground x=12 m, increases west and uses 1 m per division. Construct a time-aligned table of ground positions and B readings; mark each change's direction and identify the stationary interval. Assume straight monotone motion or rest between samples.

Scale B has zero at ground x=12 m, increases west and uses 1 m per division. Construct a time-aligned table of ground positions and B readings; mark each change's direction and identify the stationary interval. Assume straight monotone motion or rest between samples.
stages.reconstruct: x=4+2A gives 2,10,10,4 m; B=12−x gives 10,2,2,8 divisions. Changes in ground x are +8,0,−6 m (east, rest, west). B changes −8,0,+6 divisions. Rest is 2–5 s. Both encode the same physical motion.

stages.repair: Calibrate both axes from their zero and orientation, transform each row, compare signed changes and physical lengths.
stages.boundary_test: If B is relabelled with an east-positive axis and the same zero and spacing, reconstruct its readings.

A rover begins at Q=4, then moves exactly 10 m west. Recover its initial ground position, final P reading and final Q reading; check both scales describe the same displacement.
core1b.protected_work: Reconcile two incomplete coordinate logs using shared markers and a physical separation constraint.

A rover begins at Q=4, then moves exactly 10 m west. Recover its initial ground position, final P reading and final Q reading; check both scales describe the same displacement.

core1b.fresh_task: A warehouse tracker records x=−4 m, +5 m, +1 m at 0, 4, 9 s. No speed limit or between-sample direction is given. A supervisor claims distance must be 13 m; another claims 19 m is possible. Decide what the data determine, and construct an explicit route for each feasible claim.
core1b.protected_work: Choose the appropriate exact-distance or lower-bound model for a partially observed journey, and construct counterexamples.

stages.predict: Predict whether recording the middle position fixes the total travelled distance.
stages.attempt: A warehouse tracker records x=−4 m, +5 m, +1 m at 0, 4, 9 s. No speed limit or between-sample direction is given. A supervisor claims distance must be 13 m; another claims 19 m is possible. Decide what the data determine, and construct an explicit route for each feasible claim.
stages.reconstruct: Displacement is +5 m. Minimum distance |5−(−4)|+|1−5|=9+4=13 m, attained by −4→5→1. A route −4→8→5→1 has length 12+3+4=19 m; visit 8 before 4 s, then 5 at 4 s and 1 at 9 s. Thus 13 is a minimum, not a uniquely determined total.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the sampled versus actual route, a signed leg, a cumulative length or a feasibility condition.
stages.repair: Use checkpoint-wise triangle inequalities and show distinct feasible routes under the same data.
stages.boundary_test: If a sensor certifies monotone motion on each sampled interval, which claims survive?

Construct a checkpoint table of ground positions, signed changes and cumulative distance since A. Identify when it first passes x=0 and whether the end displacement equals the distance.

core1b.fresh_task: A robot starts at x=−2 m, travels east to an unknown first turning point P, then west to x=1 m, then east to x=6 m. Each leg is strictly monotone. Its total distance is 23 m. Recover P, calculate the displacement and check whether an alternative claim P=0 m could satisfy the route.
core1b.protected_work: Recover an unknown turning point by combining an exact path ledger with endpoint and reversal-order constraints.

stages.predict: Predict whether P must lie east of both the starting point and the second turn.
stages.attempt: A robot starts at x=−2 m, travels east to an unknown first turning point P, then west to x=1 m, then east to x=6 m. Each leg is strictly monotone. Its total distance is 23 m. Recover P, calculate the displacement and check whether an alternative claim P=0 m could satisfy the route.
stages.reconstruct: The first turn must exceed 1 m. D=(P+2)+(P−1)+(6−1)=2P+6=23, hence P=8.5 m. Legs 10.5,7.5,5 m total 23 m; displacement +8 m. P=0 violates the required westward leg to x=1.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the sampled versus actual route, a signed leg, a cumulative length or a feasibility condition.
stages.repair: Write the signed-order-dependent distance relation, solve for the unknown turn, then verify directions and feasibility.
stages.boundary_test: Could the same three strictly monotone legs total 8 m, with the same endpoints and second turn? Explain.

core1b.fresh_task: Two motion trackers report v=−6 m/s at t=0 and +6 m/s at t=6 s. Tracker A assumes uniform acceleration; tracker B only guarantees continuous velocity and reports its average acceleration. Decide which statements follow from both records: average acceleration, existence of a reversal, exact reversal time, and uniform acceleration. Construct a second continuous piecewise-linear v–t history with a different reversal time.
core1b.protected_work: Choose whether an interval average determines a unique reversal and speed history.

stages.predict: Predict whether the endpoint data alone determine the time at which the cart stops.
stages.attempt: Two motion trackers report v=−6 m/s at t=0 and +6 m/s at t=6 s. Decide which statements follow from both records: average acceleration, existence of a reversal, exact reversal time, and uniform acceleration. Construct a second continuous piecewise-linear v–t history with a different reversal time.
stages.reconstruct: Both have a_avg=(6−(−6))/6=+2 m/s². Continuity implies at least one zero and a sign change, not its exact time. A has v=−6+2t, zero at 3 s. B could have v=−6 at 0, 0 at 2, +6 at 6, linear on each interval, slopes +3 and +1.5 m/s². Both satisfy endpoints; neither a unique zero time nor uniform acceleration follows for B.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use explicit alternative velocity histories with identical endpoints to test a constant-acceleration assumption.
stages.boundary_test: If B certifies constant acceleration over all 6 s, what new conclusion follows?

core1b.fresh_task: A cart has a piecewise-linear velocity graph through (t in s,v in m/s): (0,−4),(2,+2),(5,+2),(7,−2). Construct an a–t step graph and a time table showing direction and whether speed increases, decreases or is constant. Give all zero-velocity times.

stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

core1b.protected_work: Reconstruct two acceleration stages using an unknown switch time and a velocity condition.

core1b.fresh_task: A cart at x=0 has u=+12 m/s and a=−3 m/s² until t=5 s, when a controller changes its motion. A sensor at x=18 m can register crossings in this interval. Decide whether v²=u²+2aΔx alone determines the number and direction of crossings; recover all valid times and signed velocities.

stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

stages.boundary_test: If the controller change occurs at t=7 s instead, recover the valid crossings.

stages.attempt: A cart starts at x=2 m with v=−3 m/s. It accelerates at +2 m/s² for 3 s, then moves with that final velocity for 2 s. Construct labelled v–t and x–t descriptions with the turning point, switch point, final position, signed displacement and total distance.

stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

Its speed is known to be between 1 and 4 m/s inclusive. Decide whether one constant speed can explain the reports; determine the period and compute distance and average velocity over the first 9 s.
core1b.protected_work: Choose arc-length versus endpoint-vector models and distinguish steady speed from steady velocity.

stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

stages.boundary_test: If the third report instead names the south point, can all three records be consistent?

Construct a table at t=0,5,10,15,20,25 s of position coordinates (east,north), instantaneous velocity direction and cumulative distance. Calculate the vector average velocity over t=5 to 25 s and over t=0 to 15 s.

Construct a table at t=0,5,10,15,20,25 s of position coordinates (east,north), instantaneous velocity direction and cumulative distance. Calculate the vector average velocity over t=5 to 25 s and over t=0 to 15 s.
stages.reconstruct: Clockwise from south: south (0,−5), west (−5,0), north (0,5), east (5,0), south, west. Tangents west,north,east,south,west,north. Cumulative arc 0, 2.5π,5π,7.5π,10π,12.5π m. From 5 to 25 s same west endpoint, average velocity zero. From 0 to15 displacement (5,5) m; average velocity (1/3,1/3) m/s.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

core1b.fresh_task: A cyclist follows a radius-8 m circle counterclockwise, starting at north. In 18 s the odometer adds 24π m. Determine the number of revolutions, period, endpoint, final tangent direction, and vector average velocity. A friend claims the endpoint must be north because 24π is a multiple of π; test the claim.
core1b.protected_work: Recover a period and speed from a partial-lap constraint and a measured route length, then combine vector and arc quantities.

stages.reconstruct: Circumference 16π m. Distance 24π implies 1.5 laps; T=18/1.5=12 s. Starting north (0,8), half-lap remainder ends south (0,−8). At south counterclockwise tangent points east. stages.boundary_test: If odometer instead adds 20π m in 18 s with unchanged radius and constant speed, recover endpoint and period.

core1b.fresh_task: A patrol robot moves east at 6 m/s for 4 s, waits for 3 s and moves west at 2 m/s for 6 s. A logger reports mean moving speed 3.6 m/s; a supervisor reports overall average speed 4 m/s by averaging 6 and 2. Decide which reports are valid for their definitions, calculate overall average speed and signed average velocity, and explain the error.
core1b.protected_work: Choose the time-weighted speed and signed-velocity model from a moving-time report and an elapsed-time report.

stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.

Construct aligned x–t and cumulative distance–time graphs, find the elapsed average speed and signed average velocity, and identify when the two graphs have opposite slope signs.

stages.reconstruct: Times 0,2,5,10,11 s; positions −4,2,2,−8,−5 m; cumulative distances 0,6,6,16,19 m. Slopes x–t +3,0,−2,+3 m/s; distance slopes +3,0,+2,+3. Opposite signs 5–10 s. Average speed 19/11 m/s, average velocity −1/11 m/s.

stages.attempt: A rail shuttle moves west at the beginning of an observation and east at its end. Its speedometer shows the same nonzero speed at both ends. The acceleration is constant and eastward throughout. An observer concludes that both the average acceleration and the net displacement must be nonzero because the shuttle changed direction. Predict what happens to net displacement if the final eastward speed is larger than the initial westward speed.
stages.reconstruct: East positive: endpoints −s,+s. The velocity change is +2s, so the average acceleration is +2s/T, nonzero and eastward. Constant acceleration gives a straight v–t segment, crossing zero halfway because endpoint magnitudes agree. The negative and positive triangles have equal magnitude, so signed area and net displacement are zero, although path is positive. If final speed exceeds initial magnitude, the positive area exceeds the negative (trapezoid mean (v_i+v_f)/2>0), so net displacement eastward. Equal speeds are not equal signed velocities; a reversal need not imply nonzero displacement.
stages.diagnose: If you set Δv=0 from equal speeds, the first error is ignoring opposite velocity directions. If you infer displacement from the fact of reversal, the first error is skipping signed areas. If you keep zero displacement after removing uniform acceleration, the first error is extending a linear-graph result to arbitrary histories. Identify your actual error or show why none applies.
stages.repair: Write −s,+s on one signed axis; explain Δv first, then the straight velocity graph and cancellation of its two triangles. Separate endpoint-guaranteed conclusions from uniform-acceleration conclusions.
stages.boundary_test: If acceleration varies during the interval but the endpoint speeds and directions stay the same, which conclusion remains guaranteed?

Both start and end at zero; the positive lobe has three times the magnitude of the negative lobe, and the negative lobe reaches −V/2. A technician says the same endpoints and the same signed area prove the carts have the same path. Explain whether the two signed areas in fact agree, then explain why the path conclusion fails. Trace a causal/physical chain from velocity sign to motion direction to signed position change and cumulative distance. Predict the effect of reflecting B's whole velocity graph in the time axis.

stages.attempt: Two carts start at the same position at rest. Cart A has a continuous triangular velocity history: rises linearly to +V at midtime and falls to zero at T. Cart B has two triangular lobes over the same T: a negative lobe on the first half, a positive lobe on the second half. Both start and end at zero; the positive lobe has three times the magnitude of the negative lobe, and the negative lobe reaches −V/2. A technician says the same endpoints and the same signed area prove the carts have the same path. Explain whether the two signed areas in fact agree, then explain why the path conclusion fails. Trace a causal/physical chain from velocity sign to motion direction to signed position change and cumulative distance. Predict the effect of reflecting B's whole velocity graph in the time axis.
stages.reconstruct: A signed area=VT/2. B negative lobe area −(T/2)(V/2)/2=−VT/8; positive peak=3V/2, positive area=3VT/8. Thus B signed area=VT/4, NOT equal to A. The premise fails as drawn. More generally even if the signed areas were equal, negative v means backward motion; signed displacement subtracts that leg while cumulative distance adds its magnitude, so an equal signed area would not prove equal path. B path=VT/2, actually equal to A's path in this specific graph despite different displacement. Reflecting B negates signed displacement (−VT/4) and interchanges directions while leaving distance VT/2 unchanged.
stages.diagnose: Wrong model A: accept the technician's equal-area assertion without checking lobe bases and heights. Wrong model B: add signed areas for cumulative distance. Wrong model C: assume equal path implies equal displacement. Point to the exact step in your first answer.
stages.repair: Make a signed-area ledger and an unsigned-area ledger. Connect the sign of each lobe to actual motion direction; verify the technician's premise before drawing conclusions. For the changed peak, repeat the ledgers and articulate why the inference still fails.
stages.boundary_test: Increase only B's positive peak to 5V/2 with the same base durations and negative lobe. What is now equal, and why is total path different?

stages.attempt: A marker moves anticlockwise at constant nonzero speed on a circle. Start at the east point. A camera compares a quarter revolution (end at north) and a half revolution (end at west), both from the same start. A student says the half-revolution average acceleration must be twice the quarter-revolution average because the marker travelled twice the arc. Explain why this reasoning fails: compare the initial and two final velocity vectors, the directions and relative magnitudes of their velocity changes, and the elapsed times. Distinguish these interval averages from the instantaneous inward acceleration at the endpoints. Predict what the average becomes over a complete revolution.
stages.reconstruct: At east v=(0,V), north v=(−V,0), west v=(0,−V). Quarter Δv=(−V,−V) (southwest, magnitude √2V); half Δv=(0,−2V) (south, magnitude 2V). The half takes twice as long; its average magnitude relative to quarter is (2V/(2t))/(√2V/t)=1/√2, smaller, not twice. Average acceleration follows vector difference divided by elapsed time, not travelled arc. Instantaneous acceleration is inward at every point, west at east, south at north, east at west, with constant magnitude V²/r; interval average directions need not equal endpoint inward direction. A complete revolution returns to the same velocity vector, so average acceleration zero despite nonzero local acceleration.
stages.diagnose: Wrong model A: use angular/arc distance instead of vector Δv in the average. Wrong model B: subtract speed magnitudes, erasing direction. Wrong model C: equate an interval-average direction with local inward direction. Identify your first such inference, or show your actual vector subtraction.
stages.repair: Rebuild the two component differences and divide each by its own elapsed time. Explain the relative magnitude using both numerator and denominator, and contrast the interval vector with local inward vectors.
stages.boundary_test: If the marker completes the same quarter arc clockwise instead, starting at east with the appropriate clockwise tangent, what is the direction of Δv and of the interval-average acceleration?

Y velocities 0,−3,2,3; signed areas −3/2,−1/2,5/2 give Δx=1/2 m; absolute areas 3/2,13/10,5/2 give D_Y=53/10 m. Same endpoint velocity +3 m/s, unequal paths. stages.attempt: A safety test uses a cart with initial speed u>0, final speed zero and total time T. Its velocity is continuous, nonnegative and piecewise linear on exactly three equal-duration intervals; every acceleration is nonpositive (coasting is allowed). The total distance is exactly half the distance uT of a reference cart. A controller limits the magnitude of every acceleration to 3u/(2T). Let S be the distance recorded in the first interval. Prove the complete interval of feasible S/(uT), including necessity and sufficiency, and recover the switch speeds and all three accelerations for S=7uT/24. A reviewer claims the half-distance measurement forces uniform braking even with this cap; decide using your design.
stages.reconstruct: Let switch speeds be w1,w2; each stage lasts h=T/3. Monotonicity requires u≥w1≥w2≥0. Three trapezoids give D=h(u+2w1+2w2)/2; D=uT/2 iff w1+w2=u. Set z=w1/u, so w2/u=1−z and z≥1/2, z≤1. Magnitudes divided by u/T are 3(1−z),3(2z−1),3(1−z). The cap 3/2 therefore gives z≥1/2 and z≤3/4. First distance S=h(u+w1)/2, hence S/(uT)=(1+z)/6∈[1/4,7/24]. Necessity follows from the equations; sufficiency: for any z in this interval choose vertices u,zu,(1−z)u,0 and linearly interpolate; all slopes satisfy cap and monotonicity and area is half. At S=7uT/24, z=3/4, w1=3u/4,w2=u/4; accelerations −3u/(4T),−3u/(2T),−3u/(4T). They are unequal, so the claimed converse fails under the stated cap. Uniform braking corresponds to z=2/3, not the endpoint design.
stages.diagnose: Wrong model A: apply the two-stage half-distance converse to three intervals (first error: two-stage hypothesis lost). Wrong model B: impose the cap only on the average acceleration (first error: it is a bound on each slope). Wrong model C: give only a necessary bound, with no construction showing sufficiency. Identify which applies to your actual saved route.
stages.repair: Derive w1+w2=u from three trapezoids, substitute z and check all three individual slope inequalities. For the entire feasible range explicitly construct the four velocity vertices and verify monotonicity, cap and area. Test the endpoint design against the claimed uniformity.
stages.boundary_test: Replace the cap by u/T, retaining every other condition. Prove the new feasible S/(uT) set and whether uniform braking is forced.

From the east point, A travels one quarter revolution anticlockwise and B one half revolution anticlockwise. A technician claims B has larger average acceleration because it travels farther. After each observation a separate controller establishes identical eastward rail velocity u at a shared local rail clock t=0. On the rails both receive the same negative rectangular acceleration pulse, one earlier for A and one later for B. Each pulse is strong enough to reverse the vehicle, and both pulses finish before the shared rail end time. A second technician says their identical final westward velocities prove identical rail displacement and total path. Explain both mistaken inferences through warranted links from tangent-vector changes and interval durations to signed velocity changes, pulse timing, direction reversal, and signed versus absolute areas. Decide which is farther east at the rail end, and whether the same reasoning determines which has greater total path.
stages.reconstruct: Circular: quarter Δv=(−V,−V), magnitude √2V in time t; half Δv=(0,−2V), magnitude 2V in time 2t; average half magnitude is 1/√2 of quarter, not larger. Instantaneous acceleration is inward throughout because tangents rotate. Rail: equal signed acceleration pulse area gives equal total Δv and equal final negative velocities; A's velocity drops earlier, so v_A≤v_B throughout and strictly less over a nonzero interval. Thus signed area difference is negative, so A ends farther west. Each reverses, and the earlier negative pulse can decrease positive-motion area while increase negative-motion area. The pointwise ordering of signed velocities does not order |v|; no universal distance ordering follows. Example instantaneous-limit pulses are not required: for identical finite pulses translated in time, shifting earlier by δ replaces δ of +u coast with δ of final −w coast. Path difference A−B=(w−u)δ, so its sign depends on the two speed magnitudes. Equal final velocities alone fix neither position nor path.
stages.diagnose: If you compare arc lengths alone, your first error precedes the vector Δv calculation. If you equate rail endpoint velocities with displacement, you omitted the velocity-history area. If you order total paths by signed velocity, you ignored reversal and |v|. Locate the first such step in your own answer.
stages.repair: Rebuild the two circular vector differences and time ratio; compare signed rail velocity histories, then compare the extra pre/post-pulse coast contributions to absolute area. State precisely when path ordering is licensed.
stages.boundary_test: If the rail pulses still occur at different times but leave both vehicles moving east at a positive final speed, explain which vehicle travels farther and why.

Determine the necessary and sufficient condition under which Z also travels uT/2. Then impose a cap |acceleration|≤3u/(2T) and derive the complete possible interval of Z's distance divided by uT, with actual admissible rate choices attaining both ends. Decide whether the two original readings force uniform braking even under the cap.

Every block has a constant nonpositive acceleration; the same rates a,b,c are used in different orders: X=(a,b,c), Y=(c,b,a), Z=(b,a,c). Two independent sensors report X and Y each travelled exactly uT/2, but Z has not yet been measured. Prove the full family of admissible rates consistent with the two readings and monotone braking. Decide whether the two original readings force uniform braking even under the cap.
stages.reconstruct: Endpoint constraint h(a+b+c)=−u. Nonpositive rates imply all histories nonnegative until zero. For three equal blocks r,s,t, D=3uh+h²(5r+3s+t)/2. X−Y=2h²(a−c); equal readings force a=c. With a=c, the order X is symmetric in acceleration: v(t)+v(T−t)=u; or substitute 2a+b=−u/h to get D_X=D_Y=uT/2. Thus a=c=−k u/T, b=−(3−2k)u/T with 0≤k≤3/2 (rates nonpositive). Z−X=h²(b−a)=uT(k−1)/3: check h²(b−a)=(T²/9)(3k−3)u/T=uT(k−1)/3. Therefore D_Z/(uT)=1/2+(k−1)/3, equals half iff k=1, uniform. Cap requires k≤3/2 and 3−2k≤3/2, hence 3/4≤k≤3/2. Z ratio ranges 5/12 to 2/3. At k=3/4, a=c=−3u/(4T), b=−3u/(2T); at k=3/2, a=c=−3u/(2T), b=0. All rates satisfy cap, endpoints and monotonicity, and every intermediate k is admissible, proving sufficiency. Two readings do not force uniform braking; any k≠1 in that interval refutes the claim.
stages.diagnose: Wrong model A: infer uniform slopes from two half readings using the two-stage theorem (first error: three-block model). Wrong model B: set all three rates equal from X=Y (first error: only a=c follows). Wrong model C: use average cap or give necessary bounds without admissible endpoint designs. Identify and cite your first error.
stages.repair: Derive the weighted area for each order and use X−Y to constrain only a=c. Parameterize the remaining rates with the endpoint constraint, derive Z−X, intersect individual cap inequalities and construct both attaining schedules. Verify sufficiency and the changed third reading.
stages.boundary_test: If Z instead reports D_Z=7uT/12 under the same cap, recover k and the three rates and decide whether the reading is feasible.
